title: Returning to Key Stage 3: Defining Curriculum Progression Before You Plan the Units
author: Sarah Findlater
summary: Sarah Findlater, continuing her Key Stage 3 curriculum series, argues that the most common curriculum design error she encounters is starting planning at the unit level and mistaking topic-level sequencing, topics that visibly get harder or more complex across year groups, for genuine progression. Her central distinction is that progression is not about topics getting harder but about a specific, nameable set of knowledge or skills getting stronger, more secure, and more transferable over time, and if a department cannot name precisely what is progressing beyond a topic label, they do not actually have a progression model. She illustrates this with a recurring experience in curriculum meetings where departments can describe exactly what topic each year group covers but fall silent when asked what skill or knowledge structure is actually meant to be stronger by the end of Year 9. Her prescribed fix is to define a progression model, two or three things that actually matter across the key stage, described at low, developing, and secure levels, before touching unit planning at all, so that units are chosen and sequenced specifically to build toward defined progression points rather than progression being an accidental byproduct of topics arranged in a plausible-feeling order.
points: Identifies topic-level sequencing (topics visibly getting harder across year groups) as a distinct and commonly mistaken substitute for genuine progression, calling it one of the most common curriculum design errors she encounters.
Defines progression precisely as a specific, nameable set of knowledge or skills getting stronger, more secure, and more transferable over time, not simply units getting more complex.

Uses a recurring curriculum-meeting scenario, departments that can describe every unit but go silent when asked what is actually progressing, to illustrate the gap between planned units and planned progression.

Prescribes defining a progression model (two or three key-stage-spanning skills described at low, developing, and secure levels) before any unit planning begins, so units are sequenced to build toward named progression points rather than progression being accidental.
quotes: Topic-level sequencing is not the same thing as progression, and treating it as though it is one of the most common curriculum design errors I encounter.
Progression is not about topics getting harder. It's about a specific, nameable set of knowledge or skills getting stronger, more secure, more flexible, more transferable, across time.

If you cannot say precisely what is progressing, what specific thing a Year 9 student can do that a Year 7 student could not, beyond simply the topic being labeled more advanced, you do not actually have a progression model.
For each of those, write out what it looks like at a low level of security, a developing level, and a secure level. This becomes your progression model.
If you can't answer that for a given unit, the unit may still be worth teaching, but it should not be described as part of a progression model, because it isn't functioning as one.
